opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time thinking about in the context of our work on emergent abilities. The short version is that if you look at the per-token probability of getting the next token right, that tends to improve pretty smoothly and predictably as you scale up models. More parameters, more data, more compute, and the cross-entropy loss goes down in a fairly regular way. That's essentially what the scaling laws literature captures.

Where things get interesting is when people take that smooth underlying improvement and evaluate it with metrics that are very harsh or discontinuous. Take exact match on a multi-step arithmetic problem, where you need every token in, say, a five-digit answer to be correct. If your per-token accuracy is p, the probability of getting the whole thing right is roughly p to the power of the sequence length. So even when p is improving steadily, that exponentiated quantity sits near zero for a long time and then shoots up. If you plot that against model scale, it looks like a sharp, unpredictable jump, and people called that an emergent ability.

Our argument was that a lot of what looked like emergence was really a function of the metric the researcher chose rather than some fundamental change in model behavior at a particular scale. When you switch to a continuous metric, like token edit distance or the log-probability of the correct answer, those same capabilities often look smooth and predictable again. And we showed you could induce apparent emergence in settings where you wouldn't expect it, like vision models, just by picking a sufficiently nonlinear metric.

Now, I want to be careful. That doesn't mean nothing interesting ever happens with scale, or that downstream behavior is always trivially predictable. Users do care about whether the answer is fully right, so those harsh metrics are meaningful for real use. But from a scientific standpoint, if you want to understand and forecast how capabilities change with size, it really helps to separate the smooth improvement in next-token prediction from the lens you use to measure it. That separation has a lot of implications for things like safety planning and deciding when to invest in scaling.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the probability of getting an entire sequence of length k right is roughly p^k, where p is per-token accuracy, and explains that this probability rises as p improves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really at the heart of the work we did on emergence, and I think the cleanest way to think about it is that there's actually a pretty smooth, well-behaved relationship underneath, and most of the drama comes from what you put on top of it.

So the basic observation, which goes back to the scaling laws literature, is that as you increase model size, the cross-entropy loss, the negative log probability of the next token, decreases smoothly and predictably. It's roughly a power law. There's nothing surprising or discontinuous happening at that level. And you can translate that directly into a per-token probability: the probability of getting any individual token correct is going up gradually, a little bit at a time, as the model gets bigger.

Now where it gets interesting is when you ask about a task rather than a token. Say a task requires the model to produce a sequence of, I don't know, ten or twenty tokens, and you only give credit if every single one is right. Exact-match accuracy. Well, now the probability of success is something like the per-token probability raised to the power of the sequence length. And if you have a quantity that's improving smoothly but you exponentiate it, you get something that looks flat for a long time and then shoots up. So a small model has per-token accuracy of, say, 0.9, and on a twenty-token answer that's about a twelve percent chance of getting the whole thing right. Bump the per-token accuracy to 0.99 and suddenly you're at eighty percent. That looks like an emergent ability. It looks like the model "couldn't do it" and then "could." But the underlying competence was changing continuously the whole time.

So the argument we made is that a lot of what gets called emergence is a property of the metric, not the model. If you swap exact match for something like token edit distance, or you look at the log-likelihood the model assigns to the correct answer instead of thresholding it, the curves become smooth and predictable again. Same models, same outputs, different lens.

I want to be careful here, because people sometimes read this as us saying nothing interesting happens with scale. That's not the claim. Larger models are clearly more capable. The claim is about predictability. If your mental model is that capabilities are smooth functions of scale, then you should be able to forecast them, and you should be suspicious of a result that says a capability appeared out of nowhere. Usually what appeared out of nowhere was a discontinuous scoring rule applied to a continuous quantity.

And I think this matters for how we think about safety and planning too. If capabilities really were unpredictable, that would be a pretty alarming situation. If they're predictable but we've been measuring them badly, that's a much more tractable problem. It says, pick your metrics carefully, look at the full distribution rather than just pass/fail, and you'll have a much better picture of what the next model is going to be able to do.

r001.rationale: The response explains that if per-token correctness is p, the chance of getting k consecutive tokens right is approximately p^k, and illustrates how a modest increase in p can sharply raise sequence-level success.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is the probability a model assigns to the next token versus whether its top prediction is correct. Those aren’t quite the same thing. You can improve the probability you assign to the observed token without changing your top prediction at all.

When we talk about scaling, we typically measure something like cross-entropy loss—how much probability the model assigns to the tokens that actually occur, averaged over a dataset. As models get larger, with sufficient data and training, that loss tends to improve in a fairly predictable way. But that doesn’t mean doubling the model size doubles the probability of getting the next token right.

And language has inherent uncertainty. There may be several perfectly reasonable ways to finish a sentence. So I’d think of size as one factor that helps a model estimate that distribution better, rather than as a direct guarantee that its next-token prediction will be correct.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes next-token probability from top-prediction correctness and discusses scaling, but it does not ask how single-token correctness relates to getting k consecutive tokens correct.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that, as you make the model larger, it gets better at predicting the next token. But we have to be a little careful about what “better” means. Usually, we’re measuring the probability the model assigns to the token that actually occurs, averaged over a lot of text. That’s different from asking whether its single most likely prediction is correct.

You can improve that probability without changing the top prediction. So a larger model might have a better loss, even when its accuracy on a particular task hasn’t changed very much. And that relationship depends on the data and training as well as the number of parameters. Size gives you more capacity; it doesn’t, by itself, guarantee a better prediction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses single-token probability and model size, but does not explain how a higher single-token probability affects the probability of correctly predicting k consecutive tokens.
